items.title: Level 1: What pre-employment checks are
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Before you start a Civil Service job, the department must carry out pre-employment checks. The offer you receive at this stage is usually called a conditional offer, which means it depends on the checks being passed. The minimum set of checks for everyone joining government is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS. BPSS is the starting standard. It is not one of the higher security clearances, and many entry-level jobs need nothing more. The aim is to make sure the department can trust that you are who you say you are and that you are allowed to do the job. The checks are carried out by the department that is hiring you, or by a team working on its behalf. You will be asked to fill in forms and send in documents. Checks can take some weeks, so reply to requests quickly and keep copies of anything you send. If something is missing, the team will usually tell you exactly what else they need. You should not hand in your notice at your current job until you have final confirmation that all checks are complete and a start date has been agreed. Until then the offer can still change, and leaving your job early could leave you without work.

questions.prompt: What is a conditional offer of a Civil Service job?

options.text: An offer that depends on the checks being passed
An offer that only applies if you pass a second interview
An offer for a job on a short fixed-term contract only
An offer that stays open for one week before it expires

questions.hint: A conditional offer is one that only becomes final once the checks are cleared.

questions.prompt: What does BPSS stand for?

options.text: Basic Public Service Scheme
Baseline Personnel Security Standard
Basic Personal Safety Statement
Baseline Pay and Staffing System

questions.hint: BPSS is the abbreviation for Baseline Personnel Security Standard.

questions.prompt: Who normally carries out the pre-employment checks?

options.text: A recruitment agency that you choose yourself
Your current employer, on behalf of the new department
The local council where you live, using its own forms
The hiring department, or a team acting for it

questions.hint: The hiring department is responsible for running the checks, directly or through a team.

questions.prompt: When should you hand in your notice at your current job?

options.text: Once all checks are passed and a start date is confirmed
As soon as you receive the conditional offer
On the day you send in your first document
Straight after your interview if it went well

questions.hint: The offer can still change until the checks finish, so wait for final confirmation.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the BPSS?

options.text: The starting standard of checks for people joining government
A training course that new starters complete in their first week
The highest level of security clearance used in government
A skills test that all candidates must pass before an interview

questions.hint: BPSS is the basic standard that all new joiners go through.

questions.prompt: Why do departments carry out pre-employment checks?

options.text: To rank all candidates by how well they did at their interview
To decide which pay band each new starter will be placed in
To find out about the political views of each new starter
To be sure you are who you say you are and can legally work

questions.hint: The checks confirm your identity and your right to do the work, not your opinions.

questions.prompt: The checks team says a document is missing. What is the best response?

options.text: Wait until your start date and bring it then
Reply promptly and send what they ask for
Ignore it, because the offer has already been made
Fill in your whole application form again from scratch

questions.hint: Quick replies keep the checks moving and avoid delaying your start date.

questions.prompt: How long can pre-employment checks take?

options.text: Always under one hour, because they are done online
Always more than a year
Often some weeks, so quick replies help
Always exactly one working day

questions.hint: Checks can take weeks, which is why you should keep your replies prompt.

items.title: Level 1: Proving who you are
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The first part of the BPSS is checking your identity. The department needs to be confident that you are the person you say you are. To do this you will usually be asked for original documents, not photocopies. Common examples are a passport, a photocard driving licence, and papers that show your address, such as a bank statement or a utility bill. The exact list is given to you by the department, so follow its instructions rather than guessing. Your name should match across your documents. If you have changed your name, for example after marriage, you may be asked for a certificate that shows the change. The checks team may look at the documents in person or, more often now, ask you to upload them or show them on a video call. They may also compare the photograph on a document with your face. Bring or send only what you are asked for, and keep your documents safe. If you do not have a passport, tell the team early. Other combinations of documents can often be accepted, and they can explain what would work for you. Never use a document that belongs to someone else, and never alter a document. Providing false identity documents is a serious matter and ends the process straight away.

questions.prompt: What is the first part of the BPSS?

options.text: Checking your bank balance
Checking your exam results
Checking your identity
Checking your health records

questions.hint: The BPSS begins by confirming that you are who you say you are.

options.text: Original documents, not photocopies

questions.hint: Departments usually want to see original documents to be sure they are genuine.

options.text: A utility bill
A passport
A payslip
A bank statement

questions.hint: A passport is a photo identity document, unlike bills and statements which mainly show an address or income.

questions.prompt: Who gives you the exact list of documents to provide?

The bank where you hold your account
The department that is hiring you

questions.hint: The hiring department sets out which documents it accepts.

options.text: A letter from your doctor
A certificate that shows the change of name
A copy of your CV with the new name added
A reference from your previous landlord

questions.hint: A certificate links your old name and your new name.

questions.prompt: If you have no passport, what is the best step to take?

options.text: Wait until your first day in the job to mention it to anyone
Leave the identity section empty and carry on with the rest

Borrow a relative's passport to use for the identity check

questions.hint: Other combinations of documents can often be accepted if you ask early.

options.text: By asking your previous employer to vouch for your name
By asking your friends to confirm who you are online

questions.prompt: What happens if someone provides a false identity document?

options.text: The process ends straight away because it is a serious matter
They are given a second attempt after a month
They are asked to correct it at their next one-to-one
The department simply ignores it if the job is junior

questions.hint: False documents are treated as a serious matter and end the process.

items.title: Level 1: Your work history
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Another part of the BPSS is your employment history. The department wants to know what you were doing, and usually looks at the past three years. This is so that it can check there are no unexplained periods. You will be asked to give the names of employers, the dates you worked there and, in many cases, contact details for someone who can confirm it. This could be a manager at a previous job. Being out of work is not a problem in itself. People take breaks to look after children, care for a relative, study, travel or look for a job. If there is a gap, you will be asked to explain it in a few words and to name someone who can confirm what you were doing, such as a teacher, a doctor, a job centre adviser or a family member in some cases. What matters is that your account is complete and true. Do not make up a job to fill a gap, and do not leave a short job off the list because you think it does not matter. Departments can find out, and leaving something out can be treated as being dishonest. If you are not sure of exact dates, say so and give your best estimate, then correct it as soon as you can find the details.

questions.prompt: How far back does the department usually look at your employment history?

options.text: About the past three years
Only your current job
About the past three weeks
Your whole life since school

questions.hint: The usual period for the history check is the last three years.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for checking your employment history?

options.text: To see how many jobs you have applied for
To find out why you left school
To work out which pay band to give you
To check there are no unexplained periods

questions.hint: The history check makes sure all of the recent period is accounted for.

questions.prompt: What are you asked to give for each past employer?

options.text: The name, dates and often someone who can confirm them
A copy of every pay slip you received while you worked there
A letter from the employer's lawyers confirming your conduct
The reason your manager chose to give you a pay rise

questions.hint: Names, dates and a contact who can confirm your time there are the usual details.

questions.prompt: How does the department treat a gap in your work history?

options.text: It treats any gap as a reason to end your application
It only accepts gaps that are shorter than one year

It only looks at gaps for people over fifty years old

questions.hint: Gaps are common; what matters is an honest explanation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a normal reason for a gap that you could explain?

options.text: Looking after children or a relative
Wanting to keep your work private
Being unable to remember the period
Not seeing the point of the question

questions.hint: Caring responsibilities are a common, accepted reason for a break.

questions.prompt: What should you do if there is a gap in your history?

options.text: Write down a job so the dates on the form run on in full
Ask the department to skip the question for you
Explain it briefly and name someone who can confirm it
Leave the dates blank in the hope that nobody notices

questions.hint: An honest explanation with someone to confirm it is the right approach.

questions.prompt: You are unsure of the exact dates you worked at a job. What is the best approach?

options.text: Say you are not sure, give a best estimate, and correct it later
Leave that job off the form altogether to be safe
Copy the dates from a friend who once worked there
Pick tidy dates so the form looks neat and complete

questions.hint: Being open about uncertainty and fixing it later keeps your record honest.

questions.prompt: Why should you not leave a short job off the list?

options.text: Leaving it out can be treated as dishonest if discovered
The department pays a bonus for full histories
The form will not allow you to continue otherwise
Short jobs earn extra points in the checks

questions.hint: Omissions can be seen as dishonesty, even for short jobs.

items.title: Level 1: Criminal record basics
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The BPSS includes a check of your criminal record. In this check the department is interested in unspent convictions. A conviction is a decision by a court that someone is guilty of an offence. Under the law, many convictions become spent after a set period of time, which means that in most situations you no longer have to declare them. Convictions that are still within that period are called unspent. A conviction being unspent does not automatically mean you cannot join the Civil Service. The department looks at what the offence was, how long ago it happened and how it relates to the job, and it decides case by case. You will normally be asked on a form to declare any unspent convictions, and a check is usually made through the official criminal records service in the part of the UK where you live. For example, in England and Wales this is often a basic check from the Disclosure and Barring Service. The most important thing is to be honest on the form. If you declare something, it can be considered. If you hide something and it is found later, the lack of honesty can be a bigger problem than the conviction. If you are unsure whether something is spent, ask the checks team or an independent advice service.

options.text: Parking tickets only

questions.hint: The BPSS looks at convictions that are still unspent.

questions.hint: A conviction is a finding of guilt by a court.

questions.hint: Spent convictions can usually be left off in most situations.

questions.hint: The department looks at the offence, the time passed and the job.

questions.hint: You declare on a form and the department verifies through official records.

options.text: The Disclosure and Barring Service

options.text: Write as little as possible

questions.hint: Declared information can be considered; hidden information is a bigger problem.

options.text: Ask a colleague who has not yet joined the department
Search online forums and follow the first answer you see

Ask the checks team or an independent advice service

questions.hint: The checks team or an independent adviser can explain the rules for your case.

items.title: Level 1: The right to work in the UK
items.body: To work in the Civil Service you must have the right to work in the UK. This is a legal requirement for all employers, not only the government. The department has to see proof of your right to work before you start the job. For a British citizen, a passport or other official documents can show this. For people from other countries, the right to work depends on your immigration status, for example settled status or a visa that allows you to work. Some people can prove their right to work through an online check run by the Home Office, using a code that they generate from their own online account. This is often called a share code. The department will tell you which method applies to you. Having the right to work is not the same as being a British citizen. Many people who are not British citizens still have the right to work in the UK. Whether you can work in a particular Civil Service job also depends on the nationality rules for that job, which are explained in the advert. If your status changes, for example if a visa has an end date, tell your employer and the checks team in good time. Do not wait for the date to pass.

items.title: Level 1: Reading the eligibility statement
items.body: Every Civil Service job advert has an eligibility statement. This says who is allowed to apply. It is the first thing you should read, before you start filling in the application. Many jobs are open to UK nationals and also to citizens of some other countries and people with certain immigration permissions. Some jobs, for example those involving national security, are reserved for UK nationals only, or for people with a specific status. The rules exist because of the nature of the work, not because of any judgement about people. The statement may also mention whether the job needs a security clearance and which level, and if it does, it may mention a period of residence in the UK. If you are not sure whether you can apply, use the contact details in the advert. The recruitment team can answer questions about eligibility. Do not guess, and do not assume that your situation is the same as someone else's, even a friend or relative. The rules depend on your own status. It is better to ask before applying than to find out after you have spent hours on an application. If you apply for a job you are not eligible for, the application will not go further, however good it is.

items.title: Level 1: What security clearance means
items.body: Security clearance is permission to work in a job that gives access to sensitive government information, places or equipment. It is decided by a process called vetting. Vetting looks into your background to judge whether you can be trusted with sensitive material. Not everybody in the Civil Service needs clearance. Many entry-level roles need only the BPSS. The jobs that do need clearance are those where the work involves more sensitive material, such as national security, policing or defence. The level of clearance depends on how sensitive the work is. A higher level means a more detailed check. The advert for a job states the level it needs, if any. You cannot apply for clearance on your own. It is requested by the organisation that employs you, which is why you only start the process after you have a job offer for a role that needs it. Clearance can take a long time, sometimes months, and a job that needs it may be offered on the condition that you obtain it. The clearance belongs to you only for as long as you need it for your job. It is linked to the role, so if you leave and your clearance is not needed, it may lapse.

items.title: Level 1: The names of the clearance levels
items.body: There are four main levels of personnel security checks in government. The first is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS. It is the pre-employment check for everyone and is the level most entry-level roles need. Above it come three security clearances, each more detailed than the one before. The first is the Counter-Terrorist Check, or CTC. It is for roles that involve working near people or places at risk from terrorism, or having some access to sensitive material. The second is Security Check, or SC. It is for roles with regular access to secret material, and it looks more deeply at your background, which can include your finances. The third and highest is Developed Vetting, or DV. It is for roles with long-term and frequent access to the most sensitive material, and it includes interviews with you and with people who know you. These levels are always written with the same names. You may see them shortened to CTC, SC and DV in adverts. Government information itself is marked with levels too, and the clearance a person needs usually matches the level of material they handle. A role only needs the level that suits it, not the highest one.

items.title: Level 1: Who is involved in clearance
items.body: Security clearance involves several people and organisations. When a job needs clearance, your employer arranges it. In the Civil Service, the department acts as the sponsor, which means it is the organisation that says you need clearance and asks for it to be carried out. The vetting itself is carried out by a specialist organisation. For most government departments this is United Kingdom Security Vetting, usually called UKSV. You will be asked to complete a security questionnaire, usually online. It asks about where you have lived, your work history, your family, and in the higher levels your money. The department's security team can answer questions about the process and will tell you what you need to do. Some people are also asked to name referees, who are people who know you well and can speak about you. Vetting staff may contact them. The staff doing the check do not make decisions about whether you can do the job. They look at the risks and give advice. The final decision on clearance is made on the basis of that advice. You will be told the outcome. If something goes wrong, there is a process for asking for a decision to be looked at again.

items.title: Level 1: Being honest on your forms
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Honesty is the most important rule in all pre-employment checks and vetting. The forms ask about your identity, your past jobs, your criminal record and, for security clearance, much more. You must give full and true answers. If you leave something out or give wrong information, the department can withdraw the job offer or refuse clearance, even if the original fact would not have mattered. A hidden fact that is found later is treated as a sign that you cannot be relied on, and trust is the thing these checks are designed to test. Being honest does not mean you will fail. Many people have things in their past that they worry about, such as debts, a conviction or a gap in work, and many of them pass because they were open. If you are unsure how to answer a question, ask the person who sent it. If you realise you have made a mistake after you have sent a form, tell the team as soon as possible, because putting it right quickly is much better than being found out. Keep a copy of everything you submit so that your answers stay consistent between forms. Do not ask other people to fill in forms for you, and do not copy answers from friends.

questions.prompt: What is the most important rule in pre-employment checks?

options.text: Using the same wording as other applicants
Giving full and honest answers
Returning forms as fast as possible
Keeping answers as short as you can

questions.hint: Full and true answers are what the checks rely on.

questions.prompt: What can happen if you give wrong information on a form?

options.text: The offer or clearance can be withdrawn
Your start date is moved a week later
You are asked to retake the interview
You are moved to a lower pay band

questions.hint: Dishonesty can lead to withdrawal of the offer or refusal of clearance.

questions.prompt: Why is a hidden fact that is found later a problem?

options.text: It suggests you cannot be relied on to tell the truth
It shows you applied for the wrong job
It means your documents must be reissued
It means the form needs a longer deadline

questions.hint: Trust is what the checks are designed to test.

questions.prompt: What is the likely result of being honest about a worry in your past?

options.text: Any worry in your past leads to refusal
Many people who are open still pass the checks
You will need to pay for an extra check
The worry is passed on to your future employers

questions.hint: Openness is valued and many people pass despite things in their past.

questions.prompt: A question on a form is unclear to you. What is the best step?

options.text: Leave it blank and submit the form
Ask the person who sent it to you
Give the answer you think looks best
Copy what a friend wrote last year

questions.hint: The sender can explain what is wanted.

questions.prompt: You spot a mistake on a form you have already sent. What is the best step?

options.text: Send a new form later in the year
Wait to see whether anyone notices
Tell the team as soon as possible
Hope it makes no difference to the result

questions.hint: Correcting a mistake quickly is far better than being found out.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep a copy of what you submit?

options.text: So that you can show it to your new colleagues
So that the department does not need to keep one
So that you can send it to your next employer
So your answers stay consistent between forms

questions.hint: Consistency helps avoid accidental differences in later forms.

questions.prompt: Who should fill in your forms?

options.text: A family member who has more time
A friend who is good at forms
You, in your own words
A paid adviser who writes them for you

questions.hint: The answers must be yours and must be true.

items.title: Level 1: Start date and contract
items.body: When your checks are complete, you receive a confirmed start date and a contract of employment. The contract sets out the main terms of the job, such as your job title, your pay, your working hours, where you will be based, how much notice you must give if you leave, and your leave. Read it carefully before you sign. If there is something you do not understand, ask the HR team before you sign, not afterwards. Your offer letter may also tell you what to do on the first day, such as where to go, what time to arrive and who to ask for, and which documents to bring. Many departments ask you to complete some extra paperwork before you start, such as bank details so that you can be paid, and tax information. Keep a copy of your contract in a safe place. Some jobs begin with a probationary period, during which your manager looks carefully at how you are settling in. If your circumstances change before your start date, for example if you need to ask for changes because of a disability or a health condition, tell the team early. They can often make arrangements before you arrive, so that you can begin well.

questions.prompt: What do you receive when your checks are complete?

options.text: A report on your interview scores
A confirmed start date and a contract
A letter naming your future promotion date
A list of the people who gave references

questions.hint: Once checks are complete, a start date and contract are confirmed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is usually set out in a contract of employment?

options.text: Your clearance application answers and referees
Job title, pay, working hours and notice period
Your interview scores and feedback from the panel
The full list of colleagues in your new team

questions.hint: Contracts set out the main terms of the job.

questions.prompt: When should you ask about something in the contract that you do not understand?

options.text: At the end of your probation
When you next have a review
Before you sign it
After your first pay day

questions.hint: Questions are best asked before you agree to the terms.

questions.prompt: What might your offer letter tell you about the first day?

options.text: How much leave you will have next year
Which projects you will lead in your first year
Where to go, what time to arrive and who to ask for
Which clearance level you will reach

questions.hint: It usually covers practical details for your arrival.

questions.prompt: Why might you be asked for bank details before you start?

options.text: So that you can pay for your own pass
So that your references can be paid
So that the department can check your savings
So that you can be paid

questions.hint: Pay is normally paid directly into your bank account.

questions.prompt: What is a probationary period?

options.text: A time when your manager looks closely at how you settle in
A period of unpaid leave before the job starts
A short exam taken during the first week
A trial week for the department to choose staff

questions.hint: Probation is when your performance and settling in are reviewed.

questions.prompt: Where is the best place to keep your copy of the contract?

options.text: With a colleague who will look after it
Somewhere safe so you can refer back to it
Nowhere, because you will not need it again
With the department, who will keep it for you

questions.hint: You may need to refer to the terms later.

questions.prompt: When should you mention that you need workplace changes because of a health condition?

options.text: Only when your condition gets worse
Only if your manager asks you directly
Early, so arrangements can be made before you start
After you have completed your probation

questions.hint: Early information lets the department prepare changes in advance.

items.title: Level 1: Your first day
items.body: Your first days in the Civil Service include an induction. This is a planned introduction to your job, your team and your department. On the first day you will usually meet your line manager, who is the person responsible for your day-to-day work and support. You will meet your team and may be shown around the building or, if you work from home, how to log in and join online meetings. You will normally be given your equipment, such as a laptop, and a pass to get into the building. You may need to show your identity documents again so that the department can see the originals. The induction explains how the department works, what the rules are about security and behaviour, and who to go to for help. You may be given a buddy, which is a colleague who helps you settle in. Nobody expects a new starter to know everything, so ask questions as often as you need. Take notes, because there is a lot of new information. Arrive on time, dress as the department advises, and bring the documents you were asked to bring. First days are usually busy and a little tiring, and that is normal.

questions.prompt: What is an induction for a new member of staff?

options.text: A planned introduction to your job, team and department
A medical check carried out by a doctor before you start
A final review of your pre-employment checks
A formal test of your job skills during week one

questions.hint: Induction helps new starters understand their role and department.

questions.prompt: Who is your line manager?

options.text: The person who arranged your security clearance for you
The person responsible for your day-to-day work and support
The most senior leader in your whole department
The colleague who happens to sit closest to you

questions.hint: The line manager supports and directs your daily work.

questions.prompt: What equipment will you normally be given?

options.text: A tool kit for repairs
A personal mobile phone to keep for life
A laptop or similar equipment for your work
A company car

questions.hint: New starters usually get the equipment needed to do their job.

questions.prompt: What is the main use of the pass you are given?

options.text: To prove your right to work to new employers
To claim travel costs back from the department
To get into the building
To access your pay details each month

questions.hint: A pass lets you enter the workplace.

questions.prompt: What might you need to show again on your first day?

options.text: Your application form
Your interview notes
Your qualification certificates
Your original identity documents

questions.hint: The department may check your original documents in person.

questions.prompt: What is a buddy for a new starter?

options.text: A trainer who teaches the mandatory courses
A senior leader who signs off your contract
A colleague who helps you settle in
An inspector who reviews your work each month

questions.hint: A buddy is a friendly point of contact for new starters.

questions.prompt: What is the right attitude to asking questions as a new starter?

options.text: Save them up until your probation review
Ask only senior leaders
Only ask once you have tried for a week
Ask as often as you need

questions.hint: Nobody expects you to know everything at the start.

questions.prompt: What does the induction explain?

options.text: How to apply for the next grade up in the first year
How to arrange your own clearance with the vetting team
How to change the terms of your contract after joining
How the department works and who to go to for help

questions.hint: It covers the department, its rules and where to get help.

items.title: Level 1: Mandatory learning
items.body: In your first weeks you will be asked to complete mandatory learning. This is training that every civil servant must do, usually online, in a short time. It covers topics that apply to everyone, so that people know the rules and can protect themselves, colleagues and the public. Common topics are security, data protection, equality and diversity, and the Civil Service Code. Security training explains how to look after information and equipment, and what to do if something goes wrong. Data protection training explains the rules for handling personal information about members of the public and colleagues. Equality and diversity training explains how to treat people fairly and respectfully. The Civil Service Code sets out the standards of behaviour expected of civil servants, which are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Your manager will tell you how long you have to finish each course. Make time to do it properly rather than clicking through, because the content is meant to help you in real situations. Your completion is recorded, and some courses must be repeated every year to keep up to date. If you have a problem with a course, for example because of a disability, ask your manager for help.

questions.prompt: What is mandatory learning?

options.text: Training only for people in senior grades
Training only for people who need clearance
Training you can choose to skip
Training that every civil servant must complete

questions.hint: Mandatory means compulsory for everyone.

questions.prompt: How is mandatory learning usually delivered?

options.text: Often online, in short courses
Only in a classroom at head office
Only through printed workbooks
Only through one-to-one coaching

questions.hint: Much of it is online and short.

questions.prompt: Which is a common mandatory learning topic?

options.text: Advanced accounting
Security
Project finance
Public speaking

questions.hint: Security is one of the usual compulsory topics.

questions.prompt: What does data protection training explain?

options.text: The rules for handling personal information
The rules for booking annual leave
The rules for claiming travel costs
The rules for using the staff canteen

questions.hint: Data protection is about personal information.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Code set out?

options.text: The rules for who can enter each building
The standards of behaviour expected of civil servants
The pay scales for each grade in the department
The dates of public holidays and closure days

questions.hint: The Code sets out values and expected behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the Civil Service Code values?

options.text: Ambition
Competition
Loyalty to the party in power
Integrity

questions.hint: The four values are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality.

questions.prompt: Why should you not simply click through the courses without reading?

options.text: Your pay depends on your course scores
Clicking quickly is not technically possible
The content is meant to help you in real situations
The courses are marked and ranked against others

questions.hint: Learning properly prepares you to act correctly.

questions.prompt: Who can you ask for help if you struggle with a course, for example because of a disability?

options.text: The training provider's complaints line
The department that ran your checks
Your line manager
The security team at the front desk

questions.hint: Your manager can arrange support.

items.title: Level 1: Your manager and your team
items.body: In your early weeks you will start to build working relationships. Your line manager is the main person you will work with. They agree your objectives, which are the goals for your work in the year, and they will meet you regularly for one-to-ones. A one-to-one is a private meeting between you and your manager to talk about your work, how you are getting on, and any support you need. Come to these meetings with questions or issues in mind. You will also have a team, who work on related tasks and will help you learn. Many teams have a regular team meeting to share news and plans. It is good to introduce yourself, learn names, and offer help when you can. Some departments have staff networks, such as groups for parents, carers, disabled colleagues, or people from particular backgrounds. Joining one is optional and can be a good way of meeting people. Remember that you are part of a team which serves the public. Keep personal and customer information confidential, and follow the rules about what you may share and where. If you are unsure whether you can share something, ask first. It is better to ask than to guess.

questions.prompt: What are work objectives?

options.text: The notes from your induction
The rules for using the building
The goals for your work over the year
The list of courses you must complete

questions.hint: Objectives set out what you aim to achieve.

questions.prompt: What is a one-to-one in the workplace?

options.text: A formal assessment carried out by a panel
A training session run by an outside trainer
A private, regular meeting between you and your manager
A meeting of the whole department

questions.hint: One-to-ones are a regular chance to talk about your work.

questions.prompt: Who agrees your objectives with you?

options.text: The security team
Your buddy
The HR helpdesk
Your line manager

questions.hint: Your manager agrees them with you.

questions.prompt: What is a good thing to bring to a one-to-one?

options.text: Your original identity documents
A list of everything you did last year
Questions or issues you want to talk about
A printed copy of your contract

questions.hint: Preparing makes the meeting more useful.

questions.prompt: What is a staff network within a department?

options.text: A group of colleagues who share a background or interest
A specialist team that runs clearance for new staff
A group of senior managers who set pay for each grade
A group of computers linked together in one office

questions.hint: Staff networks offer support and connections.

questions.prompt: How do staff networks work for new starters?

options.text: Joining is compulsory within your first month
Joining is optional and a good way to meet people
Joining is open only to managers and team leaders
Joining is only allowed for people with a disability

questions.hint: Joining a network is optional.

questions.prompt: What should you do with personal and customer information?

options.text: Share it if someone asks politely
Keep it confidential
Share it with colleagues in any team
Keep a copy at home in case of need

questions.hint: Confidentiality is a basic duty.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether you can share some information. What is the best step?

options.text: Ask first
Share it and apologise later
Share only part of it
Wait and see if anyone complains

questions.hint: It is better to ask than to guess.
